mor1: Burning or stabbing pain between your toes, or a feeling of a pebble in your shoe? What causes Morton’s neuroma, which shoes help, and when are injections or surgery needed? Four exercises to do at home.
mor3: Do you get burning or stabbing pain between your toes when walking, or feel as if there is a pebble in your shoe? Morton’s neuroma is a thickening of the tissue around a nerve between the toe bones after it has been irritated; it is most common between the 3rd and 4th toes. Despite its frightening name, it is not a tumour, and symptoms often ease with a change of shoes and simple measures.

mor17: You can wear wide, low-heeled shoes with soft soles. Avoid tight, pointy, high-heeled and thin-soled shoes.
mor19: Forefoot (metatarsal) pads or soft insoles from a pharmacy can reduce pressure on the painful area. A foot specialist can make pads tailored to you.
mor21: You can cut down on high-impact activities such as running and jumping for a while, and rest and raise your foot when you can. Losing weight if you are overweight reduces the load on the front of the foot.
mor22: Ibuprofen or paracetamol may help; you can ask your pharmacist which suits you.
mor23: Four exercises to ease the foot and calf
mor24: There is no evidence that these exercises cure the neuroma; the aim is to keep the foot and calf flexible and strong. Do not do movements that increase the pain between your toes.
mor25: Place your hands on a wall and step one leg back. Keeping the back knee straight and the heel on the floor, move your hips towards the wall until you feel a stretch in your calf.
mor26: Sit with your feet flat on the floor. First keep your heels down and lift your toes, then lower them and lift your heels instead. It moves the foot and ankle without loading the front of the foot.
mor28: No. Despite the word “neuroma” in its name, it is not a tumour. It is a thickening of the tissue around a nerve between the toe bones after the nerve has been irritated or damaged.
mor30: Comfortable shoes that are wide, low-heeled and soft-soled are recommended. It is best to avoid tight, pointy shoes, high heels and thin-soled shoes for a while, as they increase pressure on the front of the foot. Forefoot pads or soft insoles from a pharmacy may also help.
mor32: If symptoms are very severe or other treatments have not worked, a steroid injection may be considered. In a review of 25 studies, the strongest evidence for reducing pain among non-surgical treatments was for steroid injections and foot joint mobilisation by a physiotherapist; but no treatment could be shown to be a gold standard.
mor33: Most people get relief from a change of shoes and pads. Surgery is an option considered together with a foot surgeon for very severe symptoms or when other treatments have not worked.
